title: HPDT Pod15/325P — Stefan Randall Edwards (Podiatrists)
text:
Level 6, 80 The Terrace, Wellington 6011
PO Box 10509, The Terrace, Wellington 6143, New Zealand
Telephone: 64 4 381 6816 Facsimile: 64 4 381 6770
Email: dgainey@hpdt.org.nz

DECISION NO 748/Pod15/325P
UNDER the Health Practitioners Competence
Assurance Act 2003
AND
IN THE MATTER of disciplinary proceedings against
STEFAN RANDALL EDWARDS
of Tauranga, Podiatrist
BEFORE THE HEALTH PRACTITIONERS DISCIPLINARY TRIBUNAL
HEARING 9 November 2015
TRIBUNAL Mr Kenneth Johnston (Chair), Mr Tim Burns, Dr Tim Halpine,
Ms Susan Kingi and Mr Tim Sander
COUNSEL Mr Jamie Eng and Ms Trina Williams for the Professional
Conduct Committee
Mr Michael Parker and Ms Alaina Nash for the Practitioner
IN ATTENDANCE Ms Debra Gainey, Executive Officer
Ms Helen Hoffman, Stenographer

Introduction
1. A Professional Conduct Committee of the Podiatrists Board of New Zealand prefers a
professional disciplinary charge against the Practitioner pursuant to s100(1)(c) of the
Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003.
2. The Notice of Charge is dated 7 July 2015, and particularises the charge in the
following terms:
“Pursuant to section 81(2) of the Act the Committee charges that:
On 25 February 2015 Stefan Randall Edwards was found guilty at trial of
one charge of assault, contrary to section 196 of the Crimes Act 1961, this
being an offence punishable by a term of imprisonment not exceeding one
year;
And that the conviction reflects adversely on his fitness to practise as a
registered podiatrist under section 100(1)(c) of the Act.”
3. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Tribunal informed the parties that it had
concluded that the PCC had made out the charge pursuant to s100(1)(c), and of its
determination as to penalty.
4. The Tribunal’s reasons now follow.
Charge
5. Section 100(1)(c) and (2) provides:
“(1) The Tribunal may make any 1 or more of the orders authorised by
section 100(1) if, after conducting a hearing on a charge laid under
section 91 against a health practitioner, it makes 1 or more findings
that -
…
(c) the practitioner has been convicted of an offence that reflects
adversely on his or her fitness to practise;
…
1

(2) The Tribunal may make a finding under subsection (1)(c) only if the
conviction concerned -
(a) [is one of several specified offences];
(b) has been entered by any court in New Zealand or elsewhere for
an offence punishable by imprisonment for a term of 3 months
or longer.”
6. Materially, then, in a case under s100(1)(c), the PCC must establish first, that a
practitioner has been convicted of a relevant criminal offence and second, that the
conviction reflects adversely on his or her fitness to practise.
Evidence
7. The core evidence before the Tribunal was in the form of an Agreed Statement of
Facts, and we set this out in full:
MAY IT PLEASE THE TRIBUNAL:
1. The Professional Conduct Committee has laid a charge in the Tribunal
alleging that Mr Stefan Edwards has been convicted of an offence that reflects
adversely on his fitness to practise. The charge has been laid pursuant section
100(1)(c) of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003.
Professional background
2. Mr Edwards qualified with a B.Sc(Hons)Pod.Med from the University of
Brighton, United Kingdom, in 1993. He gained registration with the
Podiatrists Board of New Zealand on 12 April 1996. In November 1999 he
qualified as a Podiatric Surgeon and in 2010 gained Fellowship of the New
Zealand College of Podiatric Surgery (NZCPS). He is currently the President
of the NZCPS. He is also an international affiliate member of the American
College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons.
2

The conviction
3. The conviction referred to in the disciplinary charge is for one charge of
assault, contrary to s 196 of the Crimes Act 1961 (“the criminal charge”).
4. Mr Edwards was found guilty of the criminal charge following a judge-alone
trial in the Tauranga District Court before Judge R P Wolff on 25 February
2015. On the same day he was sentenced to pay:
(a) a fine of $1000;
(b) reparation for broken glasses of $700;
(c) emotional harm reparation of $300; and
(d) court costs of $130.
5. The following documents in respect of the criminal charge are included in the
agreed bundle of documents:
(a) the oral judgment of Judge R P Wolff dated 25 February 2015; and
(b) the notes on sentencing of Judge R P Wolff dated 25 February 2015.
6. Mr Edwards accepts that Judge Wolff’s oral judgment and notes of sentencing
together form the factual basis on which the Tribunal may consider the
disciplinary charge.”
8. The parties also filed an Agreed Bundle of Documents which included:
8.1 The judgment of District Court Judge R P Wolff dated 25 February 2015. The
criminal charge was defended by the Practitioner, apparently on the basis of
self-defence. Judge Wolff concluded that the prosecution had made out the
charge, rejecting that defence. In the course of his judgment, Judge Wolff
canvassed the facts in some detail, and was critical of the Practitioner, making
3

a number of observations which indicated that he did not regard him as having
been truthful;
8.2 Judge Wolff’s sentencing notes, also dated 25 February 2015;
8.3 A copy of the relevant entry in the criminal record recording the conviction
and the sentence imposed (essentially a fine).
9. The most succinct description of the factual background is contained in Judge Wolff’s
judgment, commencing at paragraph 17. We set out the relevant paragraphs:
“[17] Based on the evidence I have heard, I am satisfied that on the night of his
son’s recital on 5 September, Mr Edwards decided to visit the home of his former
wife. He did so by driving into the property tooting repeatedly, which had the effect of
causing the kennels operated by his former wife’s partner to become very disturbed by
the dogs who, understandably, reacted to this unusual event. Unsurprisingly, the
complainant proceeded out of his house to see what was going on. The defendant did
not stop but u-turned, left the address and, in so doing, drove over a sign related to
the kennel business on the property.
[18] I infer that that was done deliberately, as indeed was the tooting. I infer that
because this is a relationship that has been acrimonious. There has never been a visit
to that address before. The suggestion that it was to share the child’s braces I do not
accept as a reasonable explanation. I am satisfied, having heard what I have heard,
that the visit to the complainant’s address was designed purely for annoyance.
[19] The complainant, extremely unwisely and possibly stupidly, did not let it rest
there. I believe that his reaction was one beyond annoyance, which is how he
described it and he was angry. Mrs Edwards came on the journey. She says that
nothing untoward happened and that, as it transpires, was a wise thing for her to
have done. That is not to say that Mrs Edwards necessarily is a witness who would
4

give her ex-husband any credit for anything. She had a reasonable animos towards
him, including an immediate interpretation of the smell of alcohol on his breath, as
something that was, I took it, for the Court to infer was sinister.
[20] In fact, as it transpires, it is a piece of her evidence that is confirmed by the
accused. The accused himself said that he had a few drinks earlier in the evening.
But, the point is, that I do not wish to accept either the complainant or Mrs Edwards’
evidence uncritically and bear in mind that they may have an axe to grind.
[21] Mr Edwards himself says that the fact that their accounts are consistent one
with the other, does not mean they are truthful. It may be that they have a good story.
However, when that is closely examined, the consistencies in detail are not such that
raised in my mind the possibility of collusion or discussion. Even though Mrs
Edwards is not particularly favourably disposed towards Mr Edwards where she did
not see something and is not sure that it happened. She says exactly that – that she
did not see that. She does not say as someone who wanted to prevaricate might do,
“Oh, yes, that happened,” or “That probably happened.” She was very careful to say
the things that she did not see, as opposed to the matters that she had seen and heard
about.
[22] Weighing their evidence up and comparing it with the evidence of the police
officer who arrived at the scene, the nature of the injuries that the complainant
received, including the scratches and the consistency of the accounts between the
witnesses, I am satisfied that the account as described to them occurred as they
described it. Namely, that the complainant went to the address unwisely and foolishly
to talk about the incident that had just occurred.
[23] The defendant was not present. When he returned he parked his car in a way
that would prevent the Pajero, that clearly he recognised – he says he recognised it,
5

he saw it going up the hill that is why he turned round and came back – ensuring that
car remained. He then immediately approached the complainant, who was
approaching him and, without provocation punched him, five or six times. This was
not, in my view, as a result of an instinctive reactions, or of fear, or of being surprised
in the darkness.
[24] On the issue of darkness, the defendant’s evidence at one point about darkness
was that, “It was pitch black,” and at another point that he could see the reflection of
his wife’s teeth in the window.
[25] The complainant behaved badly on this occasion by going to the address and
attempting to reason. Reason was never going to prevail in these circumstances, but I
am satisfied that the complainant was assaulted before he did anything to the
defendant. That the defendant was not grabbed by the collar. That the blows were
struck. There was then a scuffle. A bear hug followed. The defendant was
restrained, allowed to get up and then tried to continue the fight. At which point the
complainant picked up a piece of wood which his partner, the defendant’s ex-wife,
told him to put down. That piece of wood was reasonably picked up in the
circumstances, was not used in any material way and certainly not struck. The
defendant was not struck by it as he alleges to the Podiatrists Board.
[26] Looking then at the questions that I need to consider in this case. What were
the circumstances as the defendant believed them to be? The defendant believed that
the complainant was visiting the address in order to argue and/or fight with him. His
attack was not a pre-emptive strike. It was simply the starting of a fight. The force
used – the six blows – were more than was required if there had been a belief that he
was under threat and, certainly the scratching to the eyes which occurred at a much
later point, was unjustified.”
6

10. The Practitioner also gave evidence.
11. He described his professional background. He then summarised the circumstances
leading up to the offence. He told the Tribunal, and we accept, that this is the first
occasion on which he has faced any form of criminal charge, or been involved in
professional disciplinary proceedings. As to the charge itself, he said that the “…
PCC alleges that I have been convicted of an offence that reflects adversely on my
fitness to practise. Whilst I concede that I have been convicted of an offence contrary
to s196 of the Crimes Act 1961, I strongly dispute that such conviction reflects
adversely on my fitness to practise.” However, through Mr Parker, he withdrew this,
conceding that the conviction reflected adversely on his fitness to practise. He then
described his family background including the circumstances of his separation from
his former wife, the dissolution of his marriage and the effect that these events had
had on the family and most particularly on the children of the marriage. Focusing on
the circumstances which led to the criminal proceedings, he said that the events of 5
September 2014 occurred “… during an emotionally stressful and acrimonious
encounter with [his] ex-wife, and her [new partner]. My behaviour that night was
deplorable and I deeply regret it. It has had a detrimental impact on an already
difficult relationship and I am sincerely remorseful about this.” He went on to say
that this behaviour on his part was “… uncharacteristic and isolated event…,” adding
that his actions were “… strictly confined to the events of that evening and the
emotional and distressing family circumstances prevailing at the time.” The
Practitioner then went on to say that there was no connection between his behaviour
on this occasion and his professional practice. He also asserted that one conviction is
not evidence of a pattern of behaviour reflecting adversely on his fitness to practise,
and disavowed any suggestion of an ongoing pattern of violence.
7

12. The Practitioner concluded this aspect of his evidence by saying that these events
arose in a purely domestic context which was against a background of “…particular
stresses associated with it.” He said that he would “… never put my clients in a
position where they, or any other member of the public at large for that matter, feel
intimidated or threatened. Indeed I have never been the subject of any allegations or
accusations of similar conduct occurring in my professional work.”
13. He then told us that because of his reaction to these events he had resolved to take
steps to try and ensure that he could manage the “… stresses and tensions
surrounding my family circumstances, and to ensure that such behaviour never
happens again. In this regard I have embarked on anger management counselling
with a registered psychologist, Hans Laven. I have found this to be extremely
beneficial and feel that I have been making good progress in managing my difficult
family relationships.”
14. The Practitioner also produced two documents, the first being a report from Mr Laven,
and the second being a personal character reference provided by a fellow podiatrist,
Mr Trevor Tillotson.
15. Having qualified himself to give expert evidence, Mr Laven said that the Practitioner
had approached him in early August 2015 requesting assistance. He then described
his assessment of the Practitioner, and the treatment he had proposed and embarked
upon with him. He said that the Practitioner had “… responded very well to treatment
to date, showing respect for and following my advice and teaching, considering
teaching matters and practising new skills between sessions, and reporting subjective
improvement.” Mr Laven concluded his report in the following terms under the
heading “Risk Assessment”:
8

“Mr Edward’s offence and its consequences appeared to be salutary and he
was focused on avoiding or escaping any situations which could place him at
further risk of offending. Although claiming provocation he took full
responsibility for his response and recognised its unacceptability. He sought
to recognise and overcome inadequacies in his management of the
circumstances over time that led to his offence. I assessed his risk of
reoffending as low.
Nothing in Mr Edward’s presentation or narrative suggested that he presented
any risk to his patients or professional conduct. His level of experience
appeared to enable him to slot quickly and effectively in to a focused role
regardless of external matters.”
Conclusion:
I recommend approximately 20 sessions to address the matters assessed, to monitor
his progress and to ascertain that any risk of reoffending remains at the lowest
possible level.”
16. Mr Tillotson qualified himself to provide a reference by outlining his personal and
professional connection with the Practitioner. He provided a very positive reference
concluding in the following terms:
“During the many years of my professional life and over the time of my
personal and professional association with Stefan Edwards I have known him
to be one of the most sincerely dedicated and professionally passionate
podiatrist practitioners that it has been my pleasure to meet and work with.
Podiatric surgery is his life. He has spared no expense in the development of
his surgical facility, its equipment, and his own personal professional
9

podiatric surgical training, in order to provide the best and safest possible
surgical experience, and environment, for his patients.
I have had the privilege of working alongside Stefan Edwards in the operating
theatre, initially when he was under my Tutelage during his NZCPS training
and later working on cases together once he became a qualified and
registered podiatric surgeon. I have always been impressed by his level of
surgical skill and operating practise and patient management and I have no
hesitation referring my own patients to him for podiatric surgery.”
Liability
17. As already stated, in the end, there was no contest in this case as to liability. The
Practitioner accepts that his conviction reflects adversely on his fitness to practise.
The Tribunal agrees. A conviction for a serious assault, even one such as this which is
unconnected with his or her professional practice, must inevitably reflect adversely on
a practitioner’s fitness to practise to one extent or another.
18. Accordingly, this case resolved itself into a question of what if any penalty the
Tribunal should impose on the Practitioner.
Penalty
19. The principles by which the Tribunal must be guided in considering penalty are well
settled. Both counsel addressed us on these. There was no material difference
between them.
20. The first issue is always whether it is appropriate for the Tribunal to impose any
penalty. Both s100, which sets out the grounds on which practitioners may be
disciplined, and s101, which outlines the penalties which the Tribunal may impose,
say that if, following a hearing, the Tribunal concludes that grounds exist on which a
practitioner may be disciplined, it may impose one or more of the penalties identified
10

in the latter provision. Obviously, there will be situations in which, although a health
practitioner has conducted himself or herself in a way which falls within one or more
of the circumstances identified in s100, the Tribunal may nevertheless conclude that
there is no need to impose a penalty. But this is not such a case. The serious nature of
the assault of which the Practitioner has been convicted takes it out of that category of
case.
21. The principles to which the Tribunal is obliged to adhere in considering penalties are
well settled:
21.1 The primary purposes of professional disciplinary proceedings are the
protection of the public and the maintenance of professional standards:1
21.2 In some cases, other purposes may have to be bought to account:2
21.3 Whilst punishment may be the inevitable outcome of the imposition of any
penalty on a practitioner, it is not itself a legitimate objective, unless tied very
clearly to the discharge of the Tribunal’s obligations relating to the protection
of the public and the maintenance of professional standards:3
21.4 The Tribunal is obliged to consider the full range of penalties available in any
case, before reaching a conclusion as to the appropriate outcome;4
21.5 The objective is to identify the least punitive outcome which reflects the
seriousness of the case and enables the Tribunal to discharge its obligations in
relation to the protection of the public and the maintenance of professional
standards;5
1 Roberts v PCC [2012] NZHC 3354 and Katamat v PCC [2012] NZHC 1633
2 Roberts (Supra)
3 Z v CAC [2009] 1 NZLR 1 (SC) and Singh v Director of Proceedings [2014] NZHC 2848
4 Patel v Dentists Disciplinary Tribunal (unreported), High Court, Auckland, Randerson J, 8 October 2002
5 Patel (Supra)
11

21.6 It is important to maintain consistency in the imposition of penalties, and
therefore to ensure that any penalty is not out of alignment with those imposed
in other cases – like cases should attract like outcomes;6
21.7 In the end, the search is for a fair, reasonable and proportionate penalty.7
22. For the PCC, Mr Eng identified three features of the case to which he submitted the
Tribunal should have particular regard in considering the appropriate outcome:
22.1 The seriousness of the offence which involved a violent attack extending to six
blows to the victim’s head and the scratching of his eyes;
22.2 The serious adverse consequences of the attack for the victim;
22.3 The Practitioner’s apparent refusal to take responsibility for his actions. In this
regard, as Mr Eng submitted, Judge Wolff’s sentencing notes refer to his
having gained a “…very unfavourable impression of the defendant’s lack of
veracity…” and the Judge concluded that the Practitioner had not been
forthright and honest with the Podiatrist’s Board when it investigated the
matter or with the Court. He added that the Practitioner’s evidence shifted to
meet the case against him as this evolved. Mr Eng submitted that this
demonstrated a lack of insight on the Practitioner’s part in relation to his
offending, and that his lack of candour was inconsistent with the standards of
integrity to be expected of a podiatrist.
23. Mr Eng acknowledged that there exist also some mitigating considerations in this
case, including the Practitioner’s previous good character, his expression of remorse
and his having voluntarily embarked on anger management counselling.
6 Roberts (Supra)
7 Roberts (Supra)
12

24. Balancing these considerations, it was Mr Eng’s submission on behalf of the PCC that
it would be open to the Tribunal to consider suspending the Practitioner’s practising
certificate.
25. He submitted that any penalty imposed “… must be sufficient enough to bring home to
[the Practitioner] the seriousness of his conduct so as to prevent the risk of future
offending and so, protect the public.”
26. In addition, Mr Eng submitted that, having regard to the fact that the Practitioner had
voluntarily embarked on a course of anger management, the Tribunal may also wish to
consider imposing conditions on his practising certificate to ensure that he saw that
through.
27. On the Practitioner’s behalf, Mr Parker submitted that the Tribunal need not place
great emphasis on the protection of the public in this case, because there is no
evidence suggesting that the Practitioner presented a threat to the public. This
submission was based primarily on the fact that the Practitioner’s offending took place
outside the professional environment.
28. He emphasised that the Practitioner, at least since the conclusion of the criminal
proceedings, had come to realise the seriousness of his offending, and taken steps to
address this by embarking on anger management counselling. He referred us of
course to Mr Laven’s conclusion that the Practitioner was making good progress in
that regard, and that the risk of his reoffending was low.
29. In relation to this point, Mr Parker effectively invited the Tribunal to impose
conditions on the Practitioner’s practising certificate of the sort contemplated by Mr
Eng requiring him to complete the anger management programme.
30. He then turned to the Tribunal’s responsibilities in terms of setting professional
standards. In relation to this, his submission was that both the criminal proceedings
13

and this professional disciplinary proceeding themselves send a strong message to
other practitioners that conduct of this sort is unacceptable and will have
consequences for practitioners. He submitted that the imposition of a censure and
conditions of the sort referred to earlier was sufficient to achieve that outcome.
31. Mr Parker also made a submission to the effect that the Tribunal need not treat
punishment as a particular objective in considering penalty. We have already
indicated that as a general proposition punishment is not to be regarded as an objective
of professional disciplinary proceedings (though it may be an inevitable outcome of
the imposition of any penalty). That is particularly so in a case such as the present
where the professional disciplinary proceeding has been preceded by criminal
proceedings where of course punishment is an important objective. We need say
nothing more on this score, except to record that we have not treated punishment as an
objective in this case.
32. Mr Parker next spoke about the need for any penalty to allow for the Practitioner’s
rehabilitation, and we accept that submission.
33. It was submitted on the Practitioner’s behalf that the penalty here ought to be
consistent with penalties in similar cases. That submission too we accept.
34. Mr Parker referred us to Ainsworth.8 That case involved a nurse who was convicted
of one count of assault under s9 of the Summary Offences Act 1981 (common assault)
as a result of having punched a patient who was in his care at the time. In the
professional disciplinary proceeding which followed, the Tribunal censured the
Practitioner and cancelled his registration. Mr Parker submitted, and the Tribunal
8 295/Nur 09/143P
14

accepts, that that case can be distinguished from the present because the practitioner
there assaulted an elderly and vulnerable patient in his care whereas the Practitioner’s
offending here occurred outside his practice and in the context of an emotionally
charged domestic situation.
35. Mr Parker also referred us to Re Janssen.9 There, the Practitioner, a dentist, was
convicted of assault with a weapon contrary to s202C of the Crimes Act 1961. The
practitioner became involved in an altercation at a casino which ended with her hitting
the victim over the head with a bottle and throwing a wine glass at his face. In the
subsequent professional disciplinary proceeding, the Tribunal concluded that the
assault was at the lower end of the scale, acknowledged the practitioner’s attempts at
rehabilitation and ordered a period of suspension which was suspended and only to
come into effect if she could not after a period of six months provide a certificate from
the New Zealand Dental Council confirming that no other complaints had been made
against her. Mr Parker’s submission was that this case was less serious than Janssen
because the practitioner here did not use a weapon of any sort. The Tribunal is
inclined to the view that Janssen and the current case are fairly comparable. Both
involved assaults by professional people outside the professional context. Whilst
Janssen involved a weapon, the attack by the Practitioner in this case was more
sustained.
36. Mr Parker’s next submission was that whilst the penalty in this case needed to reflect
the seriousness of the Practitioner’s misconduct, a censure and the imposition of
conditions would achieve that.
9 430/DH11/190P
15

37. Finally, he reminded us that our obligation is to identify the least punitive outcome
necessary to meet the seriousness of the case, and take account of the protection of the
public and the maintenance of professional standards, and ultimately to identify a
penalty which was fair, reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances.
Discussion
38. The Practitioner in this case has been convicted of a serious assault, and the Tribunal
is in no doubt that this reflects adversely on his professional standing.
39. In those circumstances, the Tribunal has felt obliged to give serious consideration to
all options available to it up to and including the cancellation of the Practitioner’s
registration or the suspension of his practising certificate.
40. However, the following aspects of the case appear to the Tribunal to militate against
the imposition of either of those more punitive outcomes:
40.1 The Practitioner is entitled to credit for his hitherto unblemished record;
40.2 It is significant that his offending occurred outside the professional context;
40.3 The Tribunal accepts that the offending occurred at a time when the
Practitioner was under considerable stress in the context of an emotionally
charged domestic situation, and was out of character;
40.4 Ultimately, the Practitioner has accepted responsibility for his actions and
sought help to ensure that they do not recur. Plainly, this has taken some time.
In this regard, we refer again to Judge Wolff’s comments about the
Practitioner’s lack of candour, and the fact that he did not seek assistance until
some months after the conclusion of the criminal proceeding. Initially, we
were inclined to think that this might suggest that his seeking assistance was an
16

attempt on his part to place himself in the best position in this proceeding.
However, we are prepared to give the Practitioner the benefit of the doubt in
relation to this, and accept that it simply took him some time to come to grips
with the reality that he had behaved in the way that he had, accept
responsibility for this and attempt to do something about it;
40.5 We have been assisted by Mr Laven’s report, and take some comfort from his
view that the Practitioner is making good progress and his conclusion that a
repetition of this behaviour by the Practitioner is unlikely.
41. Having regard to those considerations, we have reached the conclusion that the least
punitive outcome we can impose involves a censure –itself a serious penalty for this
Practitioner – and the imposition of conditions on his practising certificate requiring
him to complete the anger management course he has begun.
42. We are satisfied that those penalties are sufficient to mark the seriousness of the case,
and meet the critical objectives of protecting the public and maintaining professional
standards.
Costs
43. The Tribunal’s costs total $10,492.85. The PCC’s costs were not available at the
conclusion of the hearing. However, since then Mr Eng has filed a memorandum
dated 17 November 2015 which indicates that these total $20,028.56.
44. In a memorandum filed in response dated 2 December 2015, Ms Nash challenges the
reasonableness of the PCC’s costs. The basis for this challenge is that, unknown to
the Tribunal prior to receipt of Ms Nash’s memorandum, there were apparently three
complaints made to the Board, only one of which found its way to the Tribunal. Ms
Nash says that whilst the PCC’s total costs have been divided by three, but that from
the PCC’s formal decision dated 19 June 2015 it would appear that less time was
17

occupied by this complaint than the others, because only three paragraphs of an 82
paragraph decision addressed it. She contends, on that basis, that the PCC’s costs
associated with this matter should be 7.32% of the total.
45. Mr Eng has replied to this point in a further memorandum dated 7 December 2015.
He says that the three way division reflects the fact that “… it was not possible to
delineate the time spent on the conviction referred from the other two PCC matters
…”
46. In the Tribunal’s view it is unrealistic to attempt to apportion the PCC’s time in
accordance with the number of paragraphs devoted to each of the three complaints in
the PCC’s decision. That is simply not how these things work. In the end, we are
satisfied that a three way division, whilst not perfect, is the fairest way of reflecting
the fact that the PCC was dealing with three complaints.
47. There being no other challenge to the costs put forward by the PCC, the Tribunal has
considered the total figure, and is satisfied that the PCC’s costs are reasonable.
48. The next question is what proportion, if any, of the total costs the Respondent should
be ordered to pay.
49. It would seem to be common ground that an order for costs is appropriate. For the
PCC, Mr Eng submits that that order should reflect between 40 and 50%. For the
Practitioner, Ms Nash submits that 15 – 20% would be a more appropriate order.
50. The key issue which emerges from the parties’ memoranda is the Practitioner’s
financial position. Both accept that the starting point for consideration is an order for
half of the costs. But, on the Practitioner’s behalf, Ms Nash says that his financial
position is such that the Tribunal should exercise its discretion by making an order for
a lower proportion.
18

51. Ms Nash acknowledges that the Practitioner’s practice is “… profitable …” The
financial statements of the practice for the FYE 31 March 2016 do show a reasonably
successful business. However, Ms Nash says that the practice’s outgoings, which of
course include the proprietor’s drawings, are high, so that the practice will have a
negative cash flow overall. There is a limit to the level of detail that the Tribunal can
go into in examining practitioners’ financial affairs when considering costs. The
fundamental position in this case is that the Practitioner has a profitable practice. He
may have some judgments to make about allocation of resources over the next few
years, but the Tribunal cannot allow such matters to determine how it deals with costs.
52. Standing back from the matter, the Tribunal’s assessment is that an appropriate order
in this case would be that the Practitioner pay 40% of the Tribunal’s costs and 40% of
the PCC’s. That will result in a total cost order of approximately $12,000.00.
Suppression
53. The Practitioner seeks an order suppressing his name. This is resisted by the PCC.
54. Section 95 of the Act entitles the Tribunal to suppress aspects of its decisions –
including the names of practitioners – where the Tribunal is satisfied that it is
desirable to do so.
55. This is a case in which there has already been a criminal proceeding and in that
proceeding no suppression order was sought or made (although the Practitioner gave
evidence that his counsel in the criminal proceeding had somehow exercised his
influence to avoid any local publicity).
56. Mr Parker emphasised the interests of the Practitioner’s children, and referred us to a
number of cases which discussed the circumstances in which suppression orders are
made.
19

57. The public interest in the open administration of justice in courts and tribunal is the
orthodox starting point. The interests of a practitioner’s family are always important.
However, in our judgment, nothing in this case indicates that the Respondent’s
children are especially vulnerable, and we are confident that he and his ex-wife, as
responsible parents, can take steps to militate the effect of publication of the
Practitioner’s name.
58. In short, we have heard nothing which persuades us that an order should be made in
this case and we decline to make one.
Conclusion
59. The Tribunal imposes the following sanctions:
59.1 Pursuant to s 101(1)(d) of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act
2003, the Practitioner is censured;
59.2 Pursuant to s 101(1)(c), the following conditions are imposed on the
Practitioner:
59.2.1 The Practitioner is to continue and complete the 20 session anger
management programme proposed by Mr Laven;
59.2.2 The Practitioner is to authorise Mr Laven to provide a report to the
New Zealand Podiatrist’s Board at the conclusion of that programme,
and ensure that such a report is provided;
59.2.3 If, for any reason, Mr Laven is unable to continue to provide
counselling of the type or for the duration proposed by him, the
Practitioner is to arrange to complete a comparable programme with
another psychologist to be approved by the New Zealand Podiatrists
Board;
